Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 60:

The explanation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And they were followed by a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with ʿAd, the people of Hud﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: And ʿAd, the people of Hud, were followed in this world by anger from God and wrath, and the like of it on the Day of Resurrection, a curse upon a curse that had already befallen them from God in this world. ﴿Unquestionably, ʿAd disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with ʿAd, the people of Hud﴾ means: May God remove them far from good. [[See the explanation of "al-laʿnah" (curse) in the earlier linguistic indexes, under the root (l-ʿ-n).]] [[See the explanation of "al-buʿd" (distance) in the earlier pages, p. 335.]]

* *

It is said: "So-and-so disbelieved in his Lord" and "disbelieved in his Lord" (kafara bi-rabbihi), and "I thanked you" (shakartu laka) and "I thanked you" (shakartuka). [[See what preceded at 3:212, the like of it.]]

* *

And it has been said: the meaning of ﴿they disbelieved in their Lord﴾ is that they disbelieved in the blessing of their Lord.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. He has produced you from the earth and settled you therein, so seek His forgiveness and then repent to Him. Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive."﴾ (11:61)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, may He be exalted in remembrance, says: And We sent to Thamud their brother Salih, and he said to them: "O my people, worship Allah alone, with no partner, and devote worship to Him exclusively, to the exclusion of whatever else is worshipped as a deity. You have no deity other than Him who deserves worship from you, and divinity is due to none but Him." ﴿He has produced you from the earth﴾ means: He began your creation from the earth. [[See the explanation of "al-insha'" (producing/originating) above, 12:156, note 1, and the references there.]]

* *

He said this because He created Adam from the earth, so the address was directed to them, since that was His act toward those who descend from him.

* *

﴿And settled you therein﴾ means: He made you inhabitants (u'mmar) of it, so the meaning is: He caused you to dwell in it for the days of your lives.

* *

This is from their saying: "A man made another man 'omrā his house" (i'mar), and "it is his 'umra." ["Umra" (with a dammah, then sukun, then an open fa'), a verbal noun like "ruq'a": "a'mara al-dar" means he granted him the house to dwell in for the duration of his life, and when he died it returned to its owner. This was an act of the pre-Islamic period, which Allah annulled with Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not grant 'umra, and do not grant ruqba; whoever grants a house as 'umra or ruqba, it belongs to his heirs after him."]

* *

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said this:

18283. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah: ﴿and settled you therein﴾, he said: "He made you dwell in it (a'marakum)."

18284. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and settled you therein﴾, he says: "He made you dwell (a'marakum)."

* *

As for His words ﴿so seek His forgiveness﴾, he means: do deeds that will be a cause for Allah to cover over your sins for you, and that is faith in Him, devoting worship to Him exclusively to the exclusion of anything else, and following His Messenger Salih. ﴿Then repent to Him﴾ means: then abandon those deeds that your Lord dislikes, in favor of those He is pleased with and loves. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is near and responsive﴾ means: indeed my Lord is near to those who devote worship sincerely to Him and turn to Him in repentance, and He responds to them when they call upon Him.

**Commentary on the words of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "O Salih, you were among us a man of hope before this. Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped? Indeed, we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us."﴾ (11:62)**

Abu Ja'far said: His exalted remembrance says: Thamud said to Salih, their prophet: ﴿O Salih, you were among us a man of hope﴾, meaning: we used to hope that you would become a leader among us before this statement you made to us, that there is no god for us other than God [[See the explanation of "al-raja'" (hope) above, 4:319.]] = ﴿Do you forbid us to worship what our fathers worshipped?﴾, meaning: do you forbid us to worship the gods that our fathers used to worship? = (﴿And indeed, we are in grave doubt about that to which you invite us﴾), meaning that they do not know the truth of what he invites them to, namely the oneness of God and that divinity belongs to Him alone, sincerely.

* *

As for His saying ﴿murib﴾ (causing suspicion), it means that which gives rise to accusation, from "arabtuhu fa-ana uribuhu iraba," when I do to him something that causes him to feel doubt (rayba). [[See the explanation of "al-rayba" (doubt) in the earlier word indexes under r-y-b.]] From this is the verse of the Hudhali poet: [[He is Khalid ibn Zuhayr al-Hudhali.]]

*"I used to come to her from the unseen,*
*She sniffs at my side and strips my garment,*
*As if I had caused him doubt with suspicion."*

[[This is in Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 1:165, and in Lisan al-Arab (r-y-b), (b-z-z), (a-t-y), and elsewhere. It will also come later in the commentary 22:76 (Bulaq edition). Khalid ibn Zuhayr was the nephew (sister's son) of Abu Dhu'ayb. Abu Dhu'ayb had sent him as a messenger to his beloved, and he corrupted her for him, so Abu Dhu'ayb suspected him regarding the matter. Khalid said to him: "O people, what is my concern with Abu Dhu'ayb... I used to come to him from the unseen."

"Atawtuhu" is a dialectal form of "ataytuhu" (I came to him). His saying "min ghayb" (from the unseen) means from a place where he does not know, because "al-ghayb" is the place whose far side is unknown. "Yabuzz thawbi" means he pulls it toward himself, intending to hold it until he extracts what is hidden in his soul, because of his long-standing suspicion of him.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 63:

The explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Said he: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who will protect me from Allah if I disobey Him? You would only increase me in loss."﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Salih said to his people, Thamud: ﴿O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord﴾, meaning: if I am upon a proof and clarity from Allah, which I know and am certain of [[See the explanation of "al-bayyinah" in the earlier lexical indices under (b-y-n).]] — ﴿and He has given me mercy from Himself﴾, meaning: and He has given me from Himself prophethood, wisdom and Islam.

﴿Then who will protect me from Allah if I disobey Him?﴾, meaning: who is it that will ward off His punishment from me if He punishes me for disobeying Him, so as to rescue me from it? ﴿You would only increase me in loss﴾ — by your excuse with which you excuse yourselves, that you worship what your fathers used to worship — ﴿other than loss﴾ for you, which causes you to lose your portions of Allah's mercy. [[See the explanation of "al-khusran" in the earlier lexical indices under (kh-s-r).]] As follows:

18285 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿You would only increase me in loss﴾ — he said: you only increase in loss.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 64:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. So leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, is informing of what Salih said to his people, Thamud, when they said to him: ﴿And indeed, we are in disquiet and doubt about that to which you invite us﴾, and they asked him for a sign for what he invited them to. ﴿O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah for you as a sign﴾, meaning: a proof, a token, and an indication of the truth of what I invite you to. ﴿So leave her to eat in Allah's earth﴾, meaning: there is no obligation upon you for her provision or her upkeep. ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾, meaning: do not kill her or reach her with hamstringing. ﴿Lest a near punishment seize you﴾, meaning: if you touch her with harm, a punishment from Allah not far off will seize you and destroy you.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 65:

The explanation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿So they hamstrung her, and he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾ (65)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Thamud hamstrung the she-camel of God. In the speech there is an omitted element which has been left unmentioned, being sufficiently indicated by what is apparent, and it is: "They denied him, and they hamstrung her." Then Salih said to them: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾, meaning: enjoy your lives in the worldly abode for three days. ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾, meaning: this term which I have set for you is a promise from God, Who promised you with its expiry destruction and the descent of punishment upon you. ﴿Not to be denied﴾, meaning: he who informed you of it has not lied to you concerning it.

* *

18286- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿So they hamstrung her, and he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾ And it was mentioned to us that when Salih informed them that the punishment had come to them, they wore leather mats (anṭā') and woollen cloaks. [["Al-anṭā'" is the plural of "niṭa'" (with a kasra and then a sukun), meaning leather hide. They used to make shrouds for themselves from them, as will come at the end of hadith no. 18290, p. 377.]] And it was said to them: "The sign of that is that your complexions will turn yellow on the first day, then turn red on the second day, then turn black on the third day." And it was mentioned to us that when they hamstrung the she-camel they regretted it, and said: "Seize the young camel for yourselves!" So the young camel climbed the qarah — and "al-qarah" is the mountain — until, when the third day came, it faced the qiblah and said: "O Lord, my mother! O Lord, my mother!" three times. He said: Then the Cry was sent down at that moment.

= Ibn 'Abbas used to say: If you had climbed the qarah, you would have seen the bones of the young camel. And the dwellings of Thamud were in Hijr, between Syria and Madinah.

18287- Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, concerning ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾, he said: the remainder of their terms.

18288- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, that Ibn 'Abbas said: If you had climbed upon the qarah, you would have seen the bones of the young camel.

**Commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day. Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty﴾ (11:66)**

Abu Ja'far said: God Most High says: When Our punishment came upon Thamud, ﴿We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us﴾, meaning: by a blessing and favour from God. ﴿And from the disgrace of that Day﴾, meaning: We saved them from the humiliation and abasement of that day, by that punishment.[[See the explanation of "al-khizy" (disgrace) in the earlier lexical indexes, under (kh-z-y).]] ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Strong﴾, in His seizing: when He seizes a thing, He destroys it, as He destroyed Thamud when He seized them. ﴿The Mighty﴾: no conqueror overcomes Him, and no subduer subdues Him; rather, He overcomes and subdues everything.[[See the explanation of "al-qawiy" (the Strong) earlier, vol. 14, pp. 19, and the explanation of "al-'Aziz" (the Mighty) in the lexical indexes, under ('-z-z).]]

* *

Those who practise ta'wil (interpretation, i.e. the exegetes) have said the same as what we have said about this.

**Those who said so:**

18289. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿by mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day﴾: He said: God saved him by a mercy from Him,[[In the printed and manuscript texts: "bi-rahmatin minna" (by mercy from Us); the context requires what is adopted here.]] and saved him from the disgrace of that day.

18290. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from 'Amr ibn Kharijah, who said: We said to him: "Tell us the account of Thamud." He said: I will tell you from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about Thamud: Thamud were the people of Salih. God gave them long life in this world, so that one of them would build a dwelling of clay, which would collapse while the man was still alive. When they saw this, they carved houses out of the mountains, hewing them, cutting them out and hollowing them.[[The phrase "wa-jabuha" (and hewed them) is omitted from the printed text. "Jabu-ha" means they split and dug out the rock, making it into houses.]] They lived in comfort with their livelihoods. They said: "O Salih, ask your Lord to bring forth for us a sign that we may know you are the Messenger of God." So Salih asked his Lord, and He brought forth for them the she-camel. She had a day of drinking, and they had a known day of drinking. On her day of drinking, they would leave her and the water alone and milk her, filling every vessel, container and waterskin. And when it was their day of drinking, they would turn her away from the water, so that she drank nothing from it, and they would fill every vessel, container and waterskin. God revealed to Salih: "Your people will hamstring your she-camel!" He told them, and they said: "We would never do that!" He said: "If you do not hamstring her yourselves, soon a child will be born among you [who will hamstring her]."[[The words in brackets are from Tarikh al-Tabari.]] They said: "What is the sign of that child? By God, we will not find him without killing him!" He said: "He will be a boy, fair, blue-eyed, reddish-haired, ruddy." In the city there were two elderly, powerful and unassailable men. One of them had a son whom he would not marry to anyone, and the other had a daughter for whom he could find no equal. They met in a gathering, and one said to the other: "What prevents you from marrying your son?" He said: "I cannot find an equal for him." He said: "My daughter is an equal for him, and I will marry you to her." So he married him, and that child was born between them. In the city there were eight men who spread corruption in the land and did not do right. When Salih said to them, "Only a child among you will hamstring her," they chose eight midwives from the town and appointed with them police who went about the town. Whenever they found a woman in labour, they would look at her child: if it was a boy, they would turn him over and examine him; if it was a girl, they would leave her alone.[[In the History: "If it was a boy, they would kill him." This is not in the version given in the Tafsir, and that version is the better of the two, God willing.]] When they found that boy, the women cried out and said: "This is the one Salih the Messenger of God is looking for." The police wanted to seize him, but his two grandfathers stood between them and him, saying: "If Salih wanted this, we would kill him!" He became the most wicked of children: he grew up in a day as others grew in a week, and in a week as others grew in a month, and in a month as others grew in a year. The eight who spread corruption in the land and did not do right gathered, including the two elders, and said: "Make this boy our leader," because of his standing and the nobility of his grandfathers. So they became nine. Salih would not sleep with them in the town; he would stay at a mosque called "the Mosque of Salih," where he spent the night. When morning came he would come to them and admonish and remind them; and when evening came he would go out to his mosque and spend the night there.

= Hajjaj said: Ibn Jurayj said: When Salih told them, "A boy will be born who will be the cause of your destruction," they said: "What do you command us?" He said: "I command you to kill them!" So they killed them, all except one. When that boy grew up, they said: "If we had not killed our children, every man among us would have one like this. This is the work of Salih!" So they plotted together to kill him, saying: "We will go out as travellers, and people will see us openly. Then we will return on such and such a night of such and such a month, and we will lie in wait for him at his place of prayer and kill him. People will think only that we were travelling, as we are." So they came and entered beneath a rock, lying in wait for him. God sent the rock down upon them and crushed them, and in the morning they were crushed. Men who had learned of this went out, and when they saw them crushed, they returned crying out in the town: "O servants of God, did Salih not agree that they should command their children to be killed, until he killed them?" The people of the town then all agreed to kill the she-camel, and they all abstained from her except that tenth son.

= Then the narration returned to the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He said: They intended to deceive Salih, so they went until they came to a tunnel on Salih's path. Eight of them hid in it and said: "If he comes out against us, we will kill him, and then we will go to his family and attack them by night!" God commanded the earth, and it closed over them. They gathered and walked to the she-camel, which was standing at her watering place. The wretched one said to one of them: "Go to her and hamstring her!" He went to her, but her size overawed him, so he turned away. He sent another, and he too was overawed. Every time he sent a man, her great size daunted him, until they went to her themselves. The wretch approached and struck her hamstrings, and she fell thrashing. A man among them came to Salih and said: "Catch up with the she-camel, for she has been wounded!" Salih came, and they came out to meet him, apologizing: "O Prophet of God, it was only so-and-so who hamstrung her; we are not to blame!" He said: "See whether you can catch her colt. If you catch it, perhaps God will lift the punishment from you!" They went out seeking it. When the colt saw its mother convulsing, it climbed a short mountain called "al-Qara," and they climbed up to seize it. God revealed to the mountain, and it grew up into the sky until birds could not reach it. He said: Salih entered the town, and when the colt saw him it wept until its tears flowed. Then it faced Salih and cried out, and cried out again, and again. Salih said to his people: "Every cry has a term of a day. ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days; that is a promise not to be denied﴾. Indeed, the sign of the punishment is that on the first day your faces will become yellow, on the second red, and on the third black!" When they woke up, their faces, both small and great, male and female, looked as if they had been daubed with saffron perfume.[[" al-Khaluq" is a perfume made from saffron, in which yellow and red predominate.]] When evening came, they all cried out: "Surely one day of the term has passed, and the punishment has come upon you!" When they woke on the second day, their faces were red, as if dyed with blood. They cried out, wailed and wept, and recognized the sign of the punishment. When evening came, they all cried out: "Surely two days of the term have passed, and the punishment has come upon you!" When they woke on the third day, their faces were black, as if daubed with pitch. They all cried out: "The punishment has come upon you!" Then they wrapped themselves in shrouds and applied camphor and myrrh; their embalming was with aloes and "al-maqr,"[[" al-maqr" (with fatha then kasra) resembles aloe; it is said to be aloe itself, a bitter tree. In the printed text it is written "al-mughr" with a ghayn, which is an error.]] and their shrouds were leather mats.[[See the explanation of "al-anta'" (leather mats) earlier, p. 373, note 1.]] Then they threw themselves onto the ground,[[In the printed and manuscript texts: "bi-al-ard" (onto the ground); the History text is adopted here.]] turning their eyes, looking at the sky one moment and at the earth the next, not knowing from where the punishment would come: from above them from the sky, or from beneath their feet from the earth, in fear and terror.[[In the printed text: "khasfan wa-gharaqan" (sinking and drowning), which differs from the manuscript, where it reads "hasman wa-farqan" (undotted in the first word). In the History: "khashi'an wa-farqan", with "khashi'an" vocalized as if plural of "khashi'", and "farqan" vocalized as "furqan", which is corrupt in several respects. The reading adopted here is the correct one. "Al-jash'" (with two fatha vowels) means grief at separation from a loved one and eagerness for life. In the hadith of Mu'adh: "Mu'adh wept jash'an for the separation from the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." In the hadith of Ibn al-Khasasiyah: "I fear that when fighting arrives, my soul will be jash'-stricken and will hate death." "Al-faraq" is extreme fright.]] When they woke on the fourth day, a cry came from the sky containing the sound of every thunderbolt and the sound of everything on earth that makes a sound. Their hearts burst in their breasts, and they were found in their homes, lying prostrate.

**Notes on the report 18290:** "Hajjaj" is Hajjaj ibn Muhammad al-Misisi, reliable, whom the major collectors narrated from; he has been mentioned many times. "Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah": I do not know who this is. If it is Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Sabrah al-Qurashi, he is munkar al-hadith (a narrator of rejected reports), who transmits fabrications from reliable narrators. He was mentioned under no. 14044, where Hajjaj ibn Muhammad said: "Abu Bakr al-Sabri said to me: I have seventy thousand hadiths on the lawful and unlawful." Ahmad said: "He is nothing; he used to fabricate hadith." Moreover he did not meet Shahr ibn Hawshab, who died in 162 AH when he was sixty years old, whereas Shahr ibn Hawshab died in 100 AH or shortly after. If it is Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Maryam al-Ghassani, as al-Dhahabi mentioned in his notes on the Mustadrak, he is also matruk al-hadith (abandoned in narration), mentioned under no. 9071. I do not know whether he met Shahr, since he died in 156 AH. In the printed History of al-Tabari it is "Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman," and in some manuscript copies "Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah," matching the Tafsir. As for 'Amr ibn Kharijah ibn al-Muntafiq al-Ash'ari, he is a Companion. Al-'Askari mentioned that Shahr ibn Hawshab's hearing from him is not authenticated, and that he narrates from him through 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm al-Ash'ari. This report was transmitted by Abu Ja'far al-Tabari in his History, 1:116–118. It was also transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, 2:566–567, who said: "This is a hadith comprehensive of the mention of the destruction of the people of Thamud; Shahr ibn Hawshab alone transmitted it, and it has no chain other than this one. It is not to be dispensed with. It has a supporting report in abridged form with a sound chain, which confirms the soundness of this long hadith, according to the conditions of Muslim." Al-Dhahabi said in his notes: "Abu Bakr is weak, and he is Ibn Abi Maryam." Therefore this hadith is da'if (weak), due to the weakness of "Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah," whoever he is, and due to doubt about Shahr's transmission from 'Amr ibn Kharijah; so it is munqati' (disconnected).

18291. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I was told that when the Cry seized them, God destroyed everyone of them between the east and the west except one man who was in the Sacred Precinct of God; the sanctity of God's Precinct protected him from God's punishment. It was asked: "Who is he, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Abu Righal." The Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he came upon the town of Thamud, said to his Companions: "None of you should enter the town, nor drink of its water." He showed them the path the colt climbed when it ascended the al-Qara.

= Ibn Jurayj said: Musa ibn 'Uqbah informed me, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he came upon the town of Thamud, said: "Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping. If you are not weeping, do not enter upon them, lest there befall you what befell them."

= Ibn Jurayj said: Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) came upon al-Hijr, he praised God and extolled Him, then said: "As for what follows: do not ask your Messenger for signs. These were the people of Salih; they asked their Messenger for a sign, so he brought them the she-camel. She used to come from this mountain pass and depart by that mountain pass, and drink their water on the day of her coming."[[Report 18291: In this report there is a connected hadith: the hadith of Ibn Jurayj, from Musa ibn 'Uqbah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, which Ahmad transmitted through several chains, from 'Abd Allah ibn Dinar, from Ibn 'Umar. My brother, may God have mercy on him, cited it in the Musnad; see nos. 4561, 5225, 5342, 5404, 5441, 5645, 5705, 5931. As for the rest of the report, it is mursal (its chain omitted a Companion). Something similar from the hadith of Jabir has passed, nos. 14817–14823; see the commentary on these reports there. See also Majma' al-Zawa'id 6:194 / 7:37, from the hadith of Jabir transmitted by Ahmad and others.]]

18292. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ), when he passed through the valley of Thamud on his way to Tabuk, ordered his Companions to hasten their pace, not to stop there, and not to drink from its water, and informed them that it was a cursed valley. He said: It was also mentioned to us that a wealthy man among the people of Salih would give the needy among them what they needed for their shrouds. Each man would dig his own tomb and the tombs of his household, in anticipation of the promise of the Prophet of God Salih, who had warned them. Those who saw them spoke of them in the roads, the courtyards and the houses; among them were young and old, whom God left as a lesson and a sign.

18293. Isma'il ibn al-Mutawakkil al-Ash'ari, from the people of Homs, narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Waqid narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman ibn Khutham, who said: Abu al-Tufayl narrated to us, who said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went on the expedition to Tabuk,[[In the printed text: "ghazwat Tabuk"; this differs from the manuscript, and matches the History.]] he halted at al-Hijr and said: "O people, do not ask your Prophet for signs. These were the people of Salih; they asked their Prophet to send them a sign, so God sent them the she-camel as a sign. She used to come upon them on the day of her coming from this mountain pass, and drink their water, and on the day of their coming they would draw from it, [and she would be milked, just as they used to draw from their water before that, as milk], then she would leave by that mountain pass. They rebelled against the command of their Lord and hamstrung her. God promised them the punishment after three days, and it was a promise from God that could not be denied. So God destroyed everyone of them in the east and the west of the earth except one man, who was in God's Precinct, and the sanctity of God's Precinct protected him from God's punishment." They asked: "And who is that man, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Abu Righal."[[Report 18293: "Isma'il ibn al-Mutawakkil al-Shami al-Himsi," the teacher of al-Tabari, is mentioned in the Tahdhib. "Muhammad ibn Kathir" seems to be Muhammad ibn Kathir ibn Abi 'Ata al-Thaqafi al-Misisi al-San'ani, who is very weak. He was mentioned under nos. 4150 and 4836, and in a similar chain under no. 9492. "'Abd Allah ibn Waqid, Abu Raja' al-Harawi" is reliable, with no harm, and is mentioned in the Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/191. "'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman ibn Khutham al-Makki al-Qari" is a reliable Successor, though spoken of; the correct view is that he is reliable. He narrated from Abu al-Tufayl; see nos. 4341 and 5388. "Abu al-Tufayl" is 'Amir ibn Wathilah, mentioned many times, a late Companion. When the Messenger of God died he was eight years old; he must have heard this report from older Companions, and perhaps heard it from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. This report is somewhat weak in its chain. Abu Ja'far transmitted it in his History, 1:118, by this very same route, and I have not found it elsewhere.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verses 67–68:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who had wronged were seized by the Blast, and they became, in their homes, prone corpses﴾ [67] ﴿as if they had never prospered therein. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾ [68]

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: And there befell those who did what it was not theirs to do, namely hamstringing the she-camel of Allah and disbelieving in Him, ﴿the Blast, so they became in their homes prone corpses﴾, the deaths having overtaken them and left them lifeless in their courtyards. [[See the explanation of "al-juthum" (prostration, lying prone) earlier: 12:546, 566.]] As follows:

18294. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿so they became in their homes prone﴾: he says: they became in the morning having perished.

* *

= ﴿as if they had never prospered therein﴾: he says: as if they had never lived there nor dwelt in it. As follows:

18295. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding his saying: ﴿as if they had never prospered therein﴾: as if they had never lived there.

18296. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, the same.

* *

We have already explained this earlier with its evidences, so there is no need to repeat it. [[See the explanation of "ghanaa" earlier: 12:569, 570 / 15:56.]]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved their Lord﴾: he says: Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and denied them. [[See what preceded, p. 367.]] = ﴿Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾: he says: Unquestionably, may Allah remove Thamud far away, because the punishment descended upon them. [[See the explanation of "al-bu'd" (distance, removal) earlier, pp. 335, 367.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 69:

The exposition of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace," and it was not long before he brought a roasted calf.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: ﴿And indeed Our messengers came﴾, from among the angels, and they, as has been mentioned, were Gabriel and two other angels. It has been said that the two other angels were Michael and Israfil with him. ﴿To Abraham﴾, meaning Abraham the Friend of Allah. ﴿With good tidings﴾, meaning with glad tidings. [See the explanation of "al-bushra" in the preceding lexical indexes, under (b-sh-r).]

* *

They differed concerning that good tidings with which they came to him.

Some of them said: it was the good tidings of Isaac.

Others said: it was the good tidings of the destruction of the people of Lot.

* *

= ﴿They said, "Peace."﴾ That is: they greeted him with a greeting of peace.

* *

"Salaman" is in the accusative by the governance of "qalu" upon it, as if it were said: they said a saying and greeted with a greeting.

* *

= ﴿He said, "Peace."﴾ That is: Abraham said to them, "Peace," so "salamun" is in the nominative, meaning: "Upon you be peace," or meaning: "Peace from you."

* *

It has been reported of the Arabs that they say "silm" with the meaning of "salam," just as they said "hill and halal," and "hirm and haram." Al-Farra' mentioned that some of the Arabs recited to him: [[I do not know who said it. The verse that al-Farra' recited in the explanation of this verse is another line, not this one, as evidence for the omission of "alaykum," and it is his saying: "We said: Peace, so she shrank back from her chief, and it was nothing but the shaking of eyebrows."

As for this line here, the author of al-Lisan mentioned it under the root (k-l-l), from Ibn al-A'rabi, so perhaps al-Farra' recited it in another place.]]

"We passed by and said: Ihi, silm," so she greeted, as the clouds gather with the glittering lightning,

meaning "salam." It has also been transmitted as "kama inkalla."

* *

Some have claimed that its meaning, when read thus, is: "We are at peace with you," from "al-musalama," which is the opposite of warfare.

This is the reading of the majority of the Kufan reciters.

* *

The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Basra read it: ﴿They said, "Salaman," He said, "Salamun,"﴾ taking the reply as coming from Abraham ﷺ to them, in the manner of their greeting: "Upon you be peace."

* *

The correct view on this matter, in my opinion, is that they are two readings close in meaning, because "al-silm" may be with the meaning of "al-salam" as I have described, and "al-salam" with the meaning of "al-silm," since a greeting is hardly ever given except between people at peace and not between enemies. So when the greeting of one people to another is mentioned, and the return of the others to them, that indicates their mutual peace. Both are, moreover, readings which have been recited by a people of authority in recitation, so whichever of the two the reciter reads, he is correct in the truth.

* *

His words: ﴿And it was not long before he brought a roasted calf.﴾

* *

The original form is "mahnudh," shifted from "maf'ul" to "fa'il."

* *

The people of Arabic have differed about its meaning. Some of the Basran scholars [[this is Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an]] said the meaning of "al-mahnudh" is "the roasted," and he said: it is said from it, "hanadhtu faraski," meaning I heated it and made it sweat. For his saying he cited the verse of the rajaz poet: [[this is al-Ajjaj]]

"And they feared from its heat that it would stampede,"

[Diwan 9; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda 1:292; al-Lisan (h-n-dh), (h-r-j), from his well-known rajaz, and this verse is from verses describing a wild ass and its she-asses when summer came and they went out seeking distant water, so he said: "Until when summer became intense thirst, and they were left behind from grazing what they had licked..." "Al-amaj" is the intensity of heat and thirst, which seizes the breath. "Talazzaja al-kala'" means followed the pasture. "Al-hanadh" is intensity of heat and its burning. "Harija al-ba'ir" means it became bewildered and stumbled from the intensity of heat.]

* *

Another of them said: "Hanadha faraslahu" means he covered it with a cloth (to make it sweat), and he said: they say "hanadhahu yahnidhuhu handhan," meaning he made it sweat.

* *

Some of the Kufans said: whatever is roasted in the ground, when you dig a hole for it and bury it and cover it over, is "al-hanidh" and "al-mahnudh." He said: horses are "tuhnadh" when covers are thrown over them, some upon others, so that they sweat. He said: it is said, "If you water, then hanidh," meaning: lessen [the water], intending: give little water and much nabidh.

* *

As for the people of interpretation, they said about its meaning what I will mention, which is:

18297. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: ﴿with a roasted calf﴾, he said: "nadij" (ripe/cooked).

18298. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿a roasted calf﴾, he said: "bi-'ijl," [["al-hasil" (with fatha on the ha and kasra on the sin): the young of a cow.]] the hasil of cattle, and "al-hanidh": the roasted, cooked.

18299. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿And indeed Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings﴾ up to ﴿a roasted calf﴾, [[in the printed edition and the manuscript here it reads "wa-lamma jaat rusulunā," which is a slip of the copyist, and the correct recitation is what I have established. Likewise a slip from him appears in the text of the verse which Abu Ja'far explains, and I corrected it, without pointing it out there.]] he said: cooked, heated, cooked with stones.

18300. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada: ﴿Then he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾, and "al-hanidh": the cooked.

18301. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada: ﴿a roasted calf﴾, he said: cooked. [He said: and al-Kalbi said:] "al-hanidh" is that which is roasted in the earth. [[What is between the brackets is not in the manuscript; I have left it as it is, though I doubt it, and I think it is an addition by another copyist after the copyist of our manuscript.]]

18302. Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi related to us, from Hafs ibn Humayd, from Shamir regarding His words: ﴿So he brought a roasted calf﴾, he said: "al-hanidh" is that which drips water, and it has been roasted. Hafs said: "al-hanidh" is like the sweating of horses.

18303. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: he slaughtered it, then roasted it on hot stones, so it is "al-hanidh" when he roasted it.

18304. Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: Abu Yazid related to us, from Ya'qub, from Hafs ibn Humayd, from Shamir ibn 'Atiyya: ﴿So he brought a roasted calf﴾, he said: the roasted that drips.

18305. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Hisham related to us, saying: Ya'qub related to us, from Hafs ibn Humayd, from Shamir ibn 'Atiyya, who said: "al-hanidh" is that whose water drips and which has been roasted.

18306. Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: al-Muharibi related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: ﴿a roasted calf﴾, he said: cooked.

18307. It was related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman related to us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words: ﴿a roasted calf﴾: that which is cooked with stones.

18308. Al-Harith related to me, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz related to us, saying: Sufyan: ﴿Then he did not delay to bring a roasted calf﴾, he said: roasted.

18309. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Karim related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Samad related to me, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "hanidh," meaning: roasted.

18310. Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "al-hinadh": the cooking. [[The report 18310 is from the long narration, which Abu Ja'far related in his History 1:127. In it is "al-tahnadh," and both are among what may be added to the lexicons.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: These sayings which we have mentioned from the people of Arabic and the people of tafsir are close in meaning to one another.

* *

The position of "an" in His words: ﴿an jaa'a bi-'ijlin haneedh﴾ is in the accusative by His words: ﴿fa-ma labitha an jaa'﴾.

On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he was alarmed by them and conceived a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot"﴾ (11:70).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: When Ibrahim saw that their hands did not reach toward the calf that he had brought them, and the food he had presented to them, he disapproved of them (nakarahum). That is because, when he set his food before them (ﷺ), as has been related, they refrained from eating it, since they were not among those who eat. Their abstention from eating at Ibrahim's place, while they were his guests, was something he found objectionable. There had been no acquaintance between them, and their situation alarmed him, and he conceived a fear of them in himself.

* *

Qatadah used to say: His disapproval was of their conduct, as follows:

18311: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he was alarmed by them and conceived a fear of them﴾: The Arabs, when a guest came down upon them and did not eat of their food, would suspect that he had not come with good intentions, and that he was harboring evil in his mind.

18312: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he disapproved of them﴾: He said: When a guest came down upon them and did not eat of their food, they would suspect that he had not come with good intentions, and that he was harboring evil in his mind; then, at that point, they would be told what the guests had come for.

Others said something else about this:

18313: al-Harith narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Jundub ibn Sufyan, who said: When the guest of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) entered, he brought the calf near to them, and they began to strike with arrows in their hands, made of wood, and their hands did not reach it; he disapproved of them at that point. [[The report 18313: al-Aswad ibn Qays al-Abdi al-Bajali is trustworthy, and the group (of compilers) narrated from him; previously mentioned under no. 7440. Jundub ibn Sufyan is ascribed to his grandfather; he is Jundub ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sufyan al-Bajali, who in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) was a youth (ghulam hazwar), as he himself said, one who had reached adolescence but not yet attained maturity. He is biographed in al-Isabah and elsewhere, and in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/220, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/510.]]

* *

It is said of this: "nakartu al-shay'a unkiruhu" and "ankartuhu unkiruhu," with the same meaning. From "nakirt" and "ankirt" comes the verse of al-A'sha:

"And she disowned me, and what she disapproved of was not / among the events, except the grey hair and baldness"

[[Diwan: 72; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah 1:293; Lisan (n-k-r) and others; it will come in the tafsir 29:145 (Bulaq). Among what Abu 'Ubaydah transmits is that Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: "I composed this verse, and I seek God's forgiveness," but he did not narrate it. He recited this verse to Bashshar while he was listening, and it was said to him: "It is by al-A'sha," and he said: "This is not from his speech." I said to him: "O my master, nor did he know the qasidah." Then he said: "A blind devil." This is a story that is told, and I am doubtful about it.]]

Thus he combined both dialects in the verse. And Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"So they disapproved of it, and they fled, and the wild she-ass pressed against him, / a swift, forward-running one, and a neck-stretched, big-chested male"

[[Diwan (Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin) 1:8; Sharh al-Mufaddaliyyat: 867, and others, describing wild asses when they came to the water and heard the hunter's sound. He said: "They drank, then heard a sound beyond them / the height of the screen, and a suspicious tapping that taps..." and a whisper from a hunter girded in his garment, / in his hand a bow-stave, hoarse and cut..." He says: they heard the hunter's sound, screened by what rose from the plateau, which is "the height of the screen"; then he says they heard what alarmed them from the tapping of the bow and the sound of the string, and they heard the hunter's whisper, which is the movement that betrays him. "Al-mutalabbib" is one who has tied his garment about him. "Al-jash'" is the rod from which the bow is made. "Ajashsh" is coarse of voice. "Al-aqta'" is the plural of "qat'" (with kasra then sukun), a small blade between two blades. He says: when she heard that, she disapproved of it and fled, and the she-ass pressed against the male, meaning she drew very close to him from the intensity of her attachment. "Sat'a" means long-necked, "hadiyah" means advanced, and "hadi" means advanced, "jurshu'" means swollen in the flanks.

As for the reading "hawja' hadiyah," it means: bold and advanced.]]

* *

As for His words ﴿and he conceived a fear of them﴾, He says: he sensed fear of them in himself and concealed it. [[See the explanation of "khifah" earlier, 13:353.]] = ﴿They said, "Do not fear"﴾: He says: the angels said, when they saw the fear Ibrahim had of them: Do not fear us, and be secure, for we are angels of your Lord = ﴿"We have been sent to the people of Lot."﴾

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 71 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And his wife was standing, and she laughed﴾

Abu Ja'far said: May He be exalted in remembrance, means: ﴿And his wife﴾, Sarah, daughter of Haran ibn Nahur ibn Saruj ibn Ra'u ibn Falikh, [[Here it is "Saruj" as written in this place; elsewhere it is "Saruju" (Saruɣ), and this is the more common form.]] and she was the cousin of Abraham. ﴿Standing﴾: it has been said that she was standing behind the curtain, listening to the speech of the messengers and the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him. And it has been said that she was standing serving the messengers, while Abraham was sitting with the messengers.
* *
As for His saying, ﴿and she laughed﴾, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿and she laughed﴾, and concerning the reason for which she laughed.

Some of them said: she laughed the familiar laughter, marveling that she and her husband Abraham were serving their guests with their own hands, out of honor for them, while they were withholding from their food and not eating.
Those who said this:
18314. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: God sent the angels to destroy the people of Lot. They came walking in the form of handsome young men, until they alighted upon Abraham and were his guests. When Abraham saw them he honored them, and he turned quickly to his family and brought a fat calf, and slaughtered it, then roasted it on hot stones; it was "al-hanidh" once roasted. He came to them and sat with them, while Sarah stood serving them. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and his wife was standing while he was sitting﴾, in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud. When he brought it near them he said, "Will you not eat?" They said, "O Abraham, we do not eat food except for a price." He said, "Indeed for this there is a price!" They said, "And what is its price?" He said, "You mention the name of God over its beginning and praise Him at its end." Then Gabriel looked at Michael and said, "It is fitting that his Lord should take him as a friend (khalil)!" When Abraham saw that their hands did not reach it, meaning they did not eat, he became afraid of them and sensed fear of them. When Sarah saw that he had honored them and was standing serving them herself, she laughed and said, "How strange are these guests of ours! We serve them with our own hands out of honor for them, and they do not eat our food!" [[The report 18314: al-Tabari narrated it in his History 1: 128.]]
* *
Others said: rather, she laughed because the people of Lot were heedless, while the messengers of God had come to destroy them.
Those who said this:
18315. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: When Abraham sensed fear within himself, they told him then what they had come for. His wife laughed and marveled that a people to whom punishment had come were in heedlessness. She laughed at that and marveled. ﴿Then We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾.
18316. Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, that he said: She laughed in wonder at what the people of Lot were in of heedlessness, and at the punishment that had come upon them.
* *
Others said: rather, she laughed, thinking of them that they intended the deed of the people of Lot.
Those who said this:
18317. al-Harith narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Abu Ma'shar narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Qays, concerning His saying: ﴿And his wife was standing, and she laughed﴾, he said: When the angels came, she thought they intended to act as the people of Lot acted.
* *
Others said: rather, she laughed when she saw her husband Abraham in alarm.
Those who said this:
18318. Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Kalbi: ﴿and she laughed﴾, he said: She laughed when they alarmed Abraham, from what she saw of the alarm regarding Abraham.
* *
Others said: rather, she laughed when she was given glad tidings of Isaac, marveling that she would have a son in her old age and her husband's old age.
Those who said this:
18319. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying Ishaq said: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Samad narrated to me that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: When the angels came to Abraham, peace be upon him, and he saw them, their appearance and beauty dismayed him. They greeted him and sat with him. He stood and commanded a fat calf, which was roasted for him, and he brought the food near them ﴿then when he saw their hands not reaching it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt fear of them﴾, while Sarah was behind the tent listening. They said, "Do not fear, for We give you glad tidings of a forbearing, blessed boy!" He gave the glad tidings to his wife Sarah. She laughed and marveled: "How can I have a son when I am an old woman and he is an aged man!" They said, "Do you wonder at the command of God? He is capable of whatever He wills! God has granted him to you, so rejoice in him."
* *
Some who held this interpretation said: this is a case of the front (muqaddam) which has the meaning of the delayed (mu'akhkhar), as if the meaning of the speech according to him is: "And his wife was standing, so We gave her glad tidings of Isaac and after Isaac Jacob, and she laughed and said: 'Woe is me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman?'"
* *
Others said: rather, the meaning of His saying "she laughed" in this place is: she menstruated.
Those who said this:
18320. Sa'id ibn Amr al-Sakuni narrated to me, saying: Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid narrated to us, from Ali ibn Harun, from Amr ibn al-Azhar, from Layth, from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿she laughed﴾, he said: She menstruated, and she was about ninety-some years old. He said: and Abraham was one hundred years old. [[The report 18320: "Ali ibn Harun" was mentioned previously under no. 6521. I wrote there that I suspected him to be "Yazid ibn Harun", and this was an erroneous suspicion, indicated by this chain, where it is likewise: "Sa'id ibn Amr al-Sakuni, from Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid, from Ali ibn Harun", and such an error is hardly likely to occur given the distance between the two statements. The correct view is that "Ali ibn Harun" is unknown (majhul), for "Baqiyyah ibn al-Walid" is well known for narrating from these unknown transmitters, and he used to relate odd reports (manakir) from these unknown persons, and he would take from everyone who turned away and came. So this "Ali ibn Harun" is among those who turned away or came! As for "Amr ibn al-Azhar al-Ataki", he is a liar who fabricates hadith. Abu Sa'id al-Haddad used to say: "Amr ibn al-Azhar used to lie in replies (mujawabah)." It was said to him: "How is this?" He said: "A man gives cloth to a weaver to weave it!" He is biographed in Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/221, Tarikh Baghdad 12: 193, Mizan al-I'tidal 2: 281, and Lisan al-Mizan 4: 353. This report is thoroughly defective in all its aspects.]]
* *
Others said: rather, she laughed out of joy at being secure from them, when they said to Abraham, "Do not fear." For he had feared them, and she too had feared them just as Abraham feared them. When she felt safe, she laughed, and then they followed the glad tidings with Isaac.
* *
Some of the Kufan grammarians claimed that they had not heard "laughed" in the sense of "menstruated" from a trustworthy source. [[This is the view of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an, in his explanation of the verse.]]
* *
Some of the Basran grammarians mentioned that some people of the Hijaz told him, from some of them, that the Arabs say "the woman laughed" meaning she menstruated. He said: "Al-dahk" (laughter) has been said to mean menstruation, and some have said "al-dahk" means the bright teeth (al-thaghr), [[In the printed edition: "al-dahk al-'ajab" and in the manuscript: "al-'asab", a poor transcription; it seems the copyist did not read well the manuscript from which he copied, and the verse he cited indicates the correctness of what we have written.]] and he mentioned the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:
"He came with a mixture the people had never seen the like of, it is al-dahk except that it is the work of the bees."
[[From his Diwan (Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin) 1: 42, and Lisan (dahk), and others, from a famous poem of his, in which at its end he mentions wine and how he gathered it from the people of Egypt and Gaza, and came carrying it across the land, until he spent the night at Muzdalifah (Jam'), and Mina. He said before the verse: "So he spent the night at Jam', then he reached Mina..." "...So he arrived early in the morning seeking the mixture with the sahl." Here "ra'dan" means seeking, and "al-mizj" is honey mixed with wine, and "al-sahl" means minting dirhams. He says: when he sought that "mizj", he bought with his wealth a mizj, that is, honey, as if it were the bright teeth of a beautiful woman in its whiteness, clarity and delicacy. This is what they said, though there is something in my mind about it. Better in my view is to say that "al-dahk" in this verse is the spathe of the palm tree when it splits open to reveal what is in its inside, and it is extremely white and pure.]]
He mentioned that one of his companions recited for him, concerning "dahk" in the sense of menstruation: [[I do not know who said it.]]
"And the laughter of hares upon the rock is like the blood of the womb on the day of meeting."
[[Lisan (dahk).]]
He said: One of his companions mentioned that he had heard, from al-Kumayt:
"The hyenas laughed at the swords of Sa'd, with corpses that were neither buried nor mourned."
[[Lisan (dahk), from a famous poem of his, not found collected anywhere; and they claim that the hyena menstruates when it eats human flesh or drinks their blood. Ibn Duraid used to reject this and say: whoever has seen hyenas at their menstruation, so that he knows they menstruate?]]
He said: he means menstruation. He said: And among the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b they say: "the palm tree laughed" when it puts forth its spathe or its unripe dates. And they said: "al-dahk" is the spathe. He said: We have heard someone narrate: "He made a pool laugh", meaning he filled it until it overflowed. He said: It seems the meanings are close to one another all of them, because it is like something that fills and then overflows.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the sayings mentioned on this matter is the saying of the one who said: the meaning of His saying "she laughed" is she marveled at the heedlessness of the people of Lot concerning what the punishment of God had encompassed them with, and their heedlessness of it.
We said this is the more correct view, because it was mentioned directly after their saying to Abraham: ﴿Do not fear, for we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾. Since that is so, and there is no basis for laughter and wonder at their saying to Abraham "Do not fear," the laughter and wonder were only at the matter of the people of Lot.
* *
The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob (71)﴾
Abu Ja'far said: May He be exalted in remembrance, means: We gave glad tidings to Sarah, the wife of Abraham, as a reward from Us for her disapproval and wonder at the deed of the people of Lot ﴿of Isaac﴾, as a son for her ﴿and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, meaning: and after Isaac's son, Jacob, from her son Isaac.
* *
"Al-waraa'" in the speech of the Arabs means the son's son, and so the people of interpretation understood it.
Those who said this:
18321. Hamid ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from Amir, who said: ﴿and after Isaac, Jacob﴾: al-waraa' is the son's son.
18322. Amr ibn Ali and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, each of them saying: Abu al-Yasa' Isma'il ibn Hammad ibn Abi al-Mughirah, client of al-Ash'ari, narrated to me, saying: I was beside my grandfather Abu al-Mughirah ibn Mihran, in the mosque of Ali ibn Zayd, when al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan passed by us and said: "O Abu al-Mughirah, who is this youth?" He said: "My son, from my waraa'." Al-Hasan said: ﴿Then We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾. [[Report 18322: "Abu al-Yasa'" Isma'il ibn Hammad ibn Abi al-Mughirah, client of al-Ash'ari, I did not find in any other place. What I found was: "Isma'il ibn Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, client of al-Ash'ari," biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/1/351, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/164, and "Umar ibn Ali ibn Muqaddam" narrated from him, but "Amr ibn Ali al-Fallas" did not narrate from him, so it is not the same person. He remains unknown until we find a biography of him.]]
18323. Amr ibn Ali and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, both saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Adi narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated to us, from al-Sha'bi concerning His saying: ﴿Then We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, he said: The son's son is the "waraa'".
18324. Ishaq ibn Shahin narrated to me, saying: Khalid narrated to us, from Dawud, from Amir concerning His saying: ﴿and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, he said: "al-waraa'", the son's son.
18325. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, the like of it.
18326. al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Abu Amr al-Azdi narrated to us, who said: I heard al-Sha'bi say: The son's son: they are the children from the waraa'.
18327. al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, who said: A man came to Ibn Abbas with his son's son, and he said: "Who is this with you?" He said: "This is my son's son." He said: "This is your child from the waraa'!" He said: It seemed to displease that man, so Ibn Abbas said: Indeed God says: ﴿Then We gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, so the son's son are the "waraa'".
18328. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When Sarah laughed and said: "How strange are these guests of ours! We serve them with our own hands out of honor for them, and they do not eat our food!" Gabriel said to her: "Give glad tidings of a son whose name is Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob." She struck her face in wonder, and that is His saying: ﴿and she struck her face﴾ [Surah al-Dhariyat: 29]. And she said: (Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman, and this is my husband, an old man? Indeed this is a strange thing.) They said: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of God? The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house; indeed He is Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾. Sarah said: What is the sign of that? He said: He took a dry stick in his hand and twisted it between his fingers, and it shook green, and Abraham said: "It is for God, when slaughtered."
18329. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: ﴿she laughed﴾ meaning Sarah, when she knew of the command of God, exalted is His praise, and what she knew of the people of Lot: ﴿they gave her glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾: with a son and a son's son. She said and struck her face (it is said: she struck her forehead): ﴿Woe is me! Shall I bear a child while I am an old woman?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿Indeed He is Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾.
* *
The readers differed concerning the recitation of this. The common readers of Iraq and the Hijaz recited: ﴿وَمِنْ وَرَاءِ إِسْحَاقَ يَعْقُوبُ﴾ with "Ya'qub" in the nominative (raf'), beginning the speech anew with His saying: ﴿and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, and this, though it is a news statement beginning afresh, contains an indication of the meaning of glad tidings.
* *
Some readers of Kufa and Syria recited ﴿وَمِنْ وَرَاءِ إِسْحَاقَ يَعْقُوبَ﴾ with "Ya'qub" in the accusative (nasb).
* *
As for the Syrian among them, it is mentioned that he inclined toward the accusative for "Ya'qub" by supposing another verb concordant with the glad tidings, as if he said: "And We granted him, after Isaac, Jacob." Since "wahabna" (We granted) does not appear, the "glad tidings" governs it and it is coordinated with the position of "Isaac", since "Isaac", though genitive, has the meaning of an accusative governed by "bashsharna" in it, as the poet said: [[He is Jarir.]]
"Bring me the like of the Banu Badr for their people, or the like of the family of Manzur ibn Sayyar..."
"Or Amir ibn al-Tufayl in his mount, or al-Harith, on the day the people cried: 'O Harith!'"
[[From his Diwan: 312, 313, and Naqa'id Jarir wa al-Akhtal: 144, and Sibawayh 1: 48, 86, and al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an, in his explanation of the verse: from the choice poems of his satire against al-Akhtal, in which he says to him: "Do not boast, for God has brought you down, O squinting ones of Taghlib, house of disgrace and shame." "There is among you no arbiter whose judgment is accepted, nor a witness of the Muslims, nor one who is steadfast." Then he says the two verses, with a third verse between them: "Or like the family of Zuhayr, while the spears are straight and the horses are in a dust-cloud and a whirlwind." In this poem he boasts of the Banu Qays ibn Aylan ibn Mudar ibn Nizar all together, against the Banu Rabi'ah ibn Nizar, who are the root of al-Akhtal al-Taghlibi. He mentioned "Banu Badr", the Fazari of Qays Aylan, and "Manzur ibn Sayyar al-Fazari", and "the family of al-Zuhayr ibn Judhaymah", the 'Abs, and "Amir ibn al-Tufayl" of the Banu Ja'far ibn Kilab, and "al-Harith ibn Zalim al-Muri", of the Banu Dhubyan, then he continued mentioning the rest of the tribes of Qays.]]
* *
As for the Kufan among them, he recited it according to the interpretation of the genitive, as is reported from him, but he made it accusative because it is not inflected. The grammarians of Arabic objected to this because of the intervening of the preposition (sifah) between the conjunction and the noun. [["Sifah" here means the preposition (harf al-jarr), as has been noted many times; see the index of terms.] They said: it is wrong to say "I passed by Amr in the house and Zayd in the house" while you conjoin "Zayd" to "Amr" except by repeating the preposition and restating it; if it is not restated, the proper construction in their view is the nominative, and the accusative is permissible. If the noun is placed before the preposition, then the genitive is permissible, as when you say: "I passed by Amr in the house and Zayd in the room." Some grammarians of Basra permitted the genitive even with the preposition intervening between the conjunction and the noun.

Abu Ja'far said: Of the two readings regarding this, the one I consider most correct is the reading of the one who reads it in the nominative (raf'), because that is the well-known manner of speech among the Arabs, which scholars of the Arabic language do not reject, and it is what the readings of the major cities (al-amsar) follow. As for the accusative (nasb) in it, it has a valid grammatical basis, but I do not like to recite with it, because the Book of Allah was revealed in the most eloquent of the tongues of the Arabs, and those most entitled to know what it was revealed in are the most eloquent of them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 11, verse 72–73:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this, my husband, is an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!" They said, "Are you amazed at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious."﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: May His mention be exalted, says: Sarah said, when she was given the good news of Isaac, that she would give birth, in amazement at what had been said to her about that, since she had reached the age at which one who has reached it, of men and women, does not bear children.

* *

It is said that she was, on that day, a daughter of ninety-nine years, and Abraham was a hundred years old. The report concerning this has already been transmitted from Mujahid earlier. [See what has preceded, no. 18320.]

As for Ibn Ishaq, he said regarding this:

18330- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: Sarah was, on the day she was given the good news of Isaac, as was related to me by some of the people of knowledge, ninety years old, and Abraham was one hundred and twenty years old.

* *

= ﴿Woe to me!﴾ This is a phrase that the Arabs say when expressing amazement at a thing and disapproval of it. They say, in amazement: "Woe to his mother, what a man, how fine his legs are!" [See the explanation of "woe" (al-waylu) earlier, 2:267–269, 273.]

* *

The grammarians have differed concerning this alif in: ﴿Woe to me (yā waylatā)﴾.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: this is a true alif. When you pause, you say "yā waylatāh" (ah), and it is like the alif of lamentation (al-nudbah). It was made light so as not to be in pause, and the ha' was placed after it to make it clearer and more extended in the sound. This is because an alif, when it is between two letters, has an echo, like a sound occurring within the hollow of a thing, which reverberates in it, so it becomes fuller and clearer.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot. Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, grieving, and turning back in repentance.﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: Almighty God says: When the fear that Abraham had sensed within himself from Our messengers had left him, when he saw that their hands did not reach his food, and he felt secure that they had not intended harm to him and his family, ﴿and the good tidings had come to him﴾, concerning Isaac, he began ﴿to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾.

* *

Those who engage in exegesis have said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said so:

18331- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham﴾, he says: the fear had left him, ﴿and the good tidings had come to him﴾, concerning Isaac.

18332- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him﴾, concerning Isaac, and Jacob born of Isaac's loins, and he was reassured about what he had feared. He said: ﴿Praise be to God, who has granted me, in old age, Ishmael and Isaac. Indeed, my Lord is the Hearer of supplication﴾ [Surah Ibrahim: 39].

* *

It has also been said that the meaning is: "the good tidings had come to him" that they did not intend him (harm).

Those who said so:

18333- Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿And the good tidings had come to him﴾, he said: when they informed him that they had been sent to the people of Lot, and that they did not intend him (harm). [[After this report there is the text: "He said: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, he said: Ma'mar narrated to us, and others said..." This addition has been deleted, as it is a copyist's oversight; he copied from the beginning of the line above, then returned to the context without completing the copying.]]

* *

Others said: he was given good tidings of Isaac.

* *

As for "al-Raw'": it is fear. It is said of it: "raa'anee kadha yaruu'uni ru'an" when he feared it. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to a man: "How can you have the fear of the believer?" And from it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"Nothing frightened me but the departure of its people ... amid the dwellings, pecking at the seeds of al-Khimkhim" [[His Diwan: 123, from his well-known mu'allaqah, and before it: "If you have resolved on parting, then your camels have been loaded on a dark day." "Al-Khimkhim" is a herb with black seeds. They used to gather in spring, and when the herbage dried, the seeds of al-Khimkhim would scatter, and that was a warning of the imminence of their departure.]] meaning: what frightened me.

Those who said so:

18334- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "al-Raw'" is al-Faraq (dread).

18336- ... He said: and Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham﴾, he said: al-Faraq.

18337- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham﴾, he said: al-Faraq.

18338- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham﴾, he said: the fear had left him.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿he began to argue with Us﴾, it means: he disputed with Us. As:

18339- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿yujadilunaa﴾, he disputed with Us.

18340- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

* *

Some grammarians of Basra claimed that the meaning of His saying ﴿yujadilunaa﴾ is "yukallimunaa" (speaks with us).

He said: Because Abraham does not argue with God; rather he asks Him and makes petition to Him. [[In the printed edition: "wa yatlubu minhu" ("and seeks from Him"); the word in the manuscript is unclear because the writing of the letter ba' in "yatlubu" lies at the end of the line.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This statement is ignorance, because Almighty God informed us in His Book that he argued concerning the people of Lot. The speaker's statement "Abraham does not argue," implying that the view of one who said regarding the interpretation of ﴿yujadilunaa﴾ that it means "disputes with us," namely that Abraham disputed with his Lord, is ignorant speech. Rather, his argument was with the messengers in the form of debate with them. The meaning is: "and the good tidings had come to him; he argued with Our messengers," but when the meaning of the speech was known, "the messengers" was omitted.

* *

His argument with them was as:

18341- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi narrated to us, saying: Ja'far narrated to us, from Sa'id: ﴿yujadilunaa fi qawmi Lut﴾, he said: When Gabriel and those with him came, they said to Abraham: "We are indeed going to destroy the people of this town; its people were indeed wrongdoers." Abraham said to them: "Will you destroy a town in which there are four hundred believers?" They said: "No!" He said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are three hundred believers?" They said: "No!" He said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are two hundred believers?" They said: "No!" He said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are forty believers?" They said: "No!" He said: "Will you destroy a town in which there are fourteen believers?" They said: "No!" Abraham was counting them as fourteen because of Lot's wife; so he fell silent and his soul was reassured.

18342- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The angel said to Abraham: "If there are five in it who pray, the punishment will be lifted from them."

18343- Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿yujadilunaa fi qawmi Lut﴾: it was mentioned to us that his argument with them was that he said to them: "Tell me: if there are fifty believers in it, will you punish it?" They said: "No!" until it reached ten. He said: "Tell me: if there are ten in it, will you punish them?" They said: "No!" And these were three towns, containing whatever multitude and number God willed.

18344- Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿yujadilunaa fi qawmi Lut﴾, he said: It reached us that he said to them that day: "Tell me: if there are fifty Muslims in it?" They said: "If there are fifty, we will not punish them." He said: "Forty?" They said: "And forty!" He said: "Thirty?" They said: "Thirty!" until he reached ten. They said: "And if there are ten in them!" He said: "A people in which there are not ten, in which there is goodness..." Ibn Abd al-A'la said: Muhammad ibn Thawr said: Ma'mar said: It reached us that there were four thousand thousand people in the town of Lot, or whatever number God willed.

18345- Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him﴾, he said: "What is your business, O messengers?" They said: "We have been sent to the people of Lot." He argued with them concerning the people of Lot, saying: "Tell me: if there are a hundred Muslims in it, will you destroy them?" They said: "No!" He kept lowering the number until it reached ten Muslims. They said: "We will not punish them if there are ten Muslims in it." Then they said: "O Abraham, turn away from this; there is in it only one household of believers," namely Lot and his household. This is the saying of God: ﴿He argued with Us concerning the people of Lot.﴾ Then the angels said: ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this; indeed the command of your Lord has come, and indeed there will come upon them a punishment that cannot be turned back.﴾

18346- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: ﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the good tidings had come to him﴾, meaning: Abraham argued on behalf of the people of Lot to turn away the punishment from them. He said: The people of the Torah claim that Abraham's argument with them, when he disputed with them concerning the people of Lot to turn away the punishment from them, was that he said to the messengers in what he spoke to them: "Tell me: if there are a hundred believers in it, will you destroy them?" They said: "No!" He said: "Tell me: if they are ninety?" They said: "No!" He said: "Tell me: if they are eighty?" They said: "No!" He said: "Tell me: if they are seventy?" They said: "No!" He said: "Tell me: if they are sixty?" They said: "No!" He said: "Tell me: if they are fifty?" They said: "No!" He said: "Tell me: if there is one Muslim man?" They said: "No!" He said: Since they did not tell Abraham that there was one believer in it, ﴿he said: "Indeed, in it is Lot,"﴾ by which he would ward off the punishment from them. ﴿They said: "We know best who is in it; we will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she is among those who remain behind."﴾ ﴿They said: "O Abraham, turn away from this; indeed the command of your Lord has come, and indeed there will come upon them a punishment that cannot be turned back."﴾

18347- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Abraham said: "Will you destroy them if you find in it a hundred believers, then ninety?" until it descended to five. He said: In the town of Lot there were four thousand thousand.

18348- Muhammad ibn Awf narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Mughirah narrated to us, saying: Safwan narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Mathna and Muslim Abu al-Habil al-Ash'ari narrated to us, both saying: "So when fear had left Abraham," to the end of the verse. Abraham said: "Will you punish a great world of Your world, in which there are a hundred men?" He said: "No, by My might, nor fifty!" He said: "Then forty? Then thirty?" until he reached five. He said: "No! By My might, I will not punish them, even if there are five in it who worship Me!" Almighty and Majestic God said: ﴿But We found in it none but one house of the Muslims﴾ [Surah al-Dhariyat: 36], that is, Lot and his two daughters. He said: Then the punishment befell them. And "Abu al-Mughirah" is: "Abd al-Quddus ibn al-Hajjaj al-Khawlani," who has appeared repeatedly, among them: 13108.

And "Safwan" is: "Safwan ibn Amr ibn Harim al-Sakuni," who has appeared repeatedly, among them: 13108.

"Abu al-Mathna" appears to mean: Muslim ibn al-Mathna al-Kufi al-Mu'adhdhin, who narrated from Ibn Umar, biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/1/256, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/195. The Arabs hardly follow "lamma" with a past-tense verb unless it is also a past. They say: "lamma qama qumtu" (when he stood, I stood), and they hardly say "lamma qama aqumu."
